full_text:
Come with me into the world of PlzDontKillUs, a bold new AI x-risk communication accelerator program that just finished its first cohort.

PlzDontKillUs took the influencer-house formula and moved it to Berkeley, giving creators personal mentorship from AI safety experts like Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares. With 57 people making daily videos for a month, the program racked up over 100 million views.

Find out how Aella, an independent sex researcher, and Ronny Fernandez, a generalist at Lightcone Infrastructure, teamed up to run the largest ever creator bootcamp focused on AI x-risk reduction.

Then meet three of the program’s top creators: Avalon Warren, Avisha NessAiver, and Josh Thor.

We do a post-mortem on PDKU and ask: Was it effective? What are creators taking from it, and do they have complaints? And does doomerism really boost view counts? PlzDoEnjoyOur special episode on PlzDontKillUs!

The Origin of PlzDontKillUs

Liron 00:14:46

So how do we blow open the doors here, where people who just reach normal audiences—the kind of audience who are just talking to their relatives about AI water use, which we don’t see as the most important issue by a long shot—how do we break into their bubbles?” Is that where you’re going with Please Don’t Kill Us?

Aella 00:15:14
Yeah. Well, the origin was maybe less intentional. I’ve always been kind of adjacent to x-risk people working on this stuff, and always felt like I didn’t really have a place in it. I’m not technical. I’m a good sex worker, right? I just write a blog. I have nothing that I can really offer these people who are significantly smarter than me, and I sort of thought that everybody had it handled. I’m like, “If I go in and try to do it, there are probably already people thinking about doing it better.”

And then it started when, I think last year, I was sitting and actually listening to some people on a speaker call about planning a party where they were trying to educate people about x-risk, but it was for complete normies. And the thing that I heard was, “Okay, so should the presentation be 45 minutes or an hour and a half?” For a party for normies.

And I was like, “I don’t know what’s happening, but I know that that’s wrong. I know you cannot invite fancy people in LA to a party and then just sit them down and give them a presentation. This is not how you convince people. This is really boring. This makes us look uncool and lame, and people don’t wanna be associated with people who are uncool and lame.”

And then I just kind of elbowed my way into helping plan things. And after this, I was like, “Okay, wait. I feel like I’m surrounded by some kind of social incompetence.
